items.title: Claude Mythos Preview: a fenced-off peak
items.what: Anthropic announced Claude Mythos Preview with Project Glasswing, giving it only to 12 launch partners and 40-plus organizations that maintain critical software, to find and fix vulnerabilities.
items.why: A major lab said outright that a model was too good at cyberattacks to release widely. The “thousands of vulnerabilities” figure is the company’s own; on May 7, 2026, Mozilla reported that Firefox 150 fixed 271 bugs it had found.

items.title: DeepSeek V4 Preview ships open weights
items.what: DeepSeek released previews of two very large models, V4-Pro and V4-Flash, and lets anyone download the whole model (open weights, on Hugging Face).
items.why: A very large model that anyone can download, run and inspect: the summit doesn’t belong only to labs that keep their models closed.

items.title: Google releases Gemini 3.6 Flash
items.what: Google launched Gemini 3.6 Flash, a fast, cheap version. Google says it writes about 17% fewer words than the previous version for the same task.
items.why: The race isn’t only about the biggest model: fast, cheap, token-thrifty versions are what many people use every day.

items.title: OpenAI releases GPT-6 Astra in stages
items.what: OpenAI released GPT-6 Astra to a select group of customers first, widening access later. According to the company’s technical document (system card), it is OpenAI’s first model rated at the highest danger level (“Critical”) for hacking.
items.why: Another lab chose a controlled release out of concern about cyberattack capability — a trend of 2026.

items.title: Anthropic releases Claude Opus 5.5, then Sonnet 5.5
items.what: Anthropic released Claude Opus 5.5 on Sept 22 and Sonnet 5.5 on Sept 28, 2026. It says Opus 5.5 costs about 40% less than Opus 5 on typical tasks.
items.why: Practice for reading the news: “40% cheaper” is the company’s own measurement at default settings — wait for users and outsiders to check it.

items.title: OpenAI announces a Navier–Stokes proof
items.what: OpenAI says about 10,000 agents running on an internal model proved that Navier–Stokes flow can “blow up”, with a version checked in Lean. The Buckmaster–Alpöge team posted a closely related result about 12 hours earlier.
items.why: If it holds, it solves a Millennium Prize Problem ($1 million). The Clay Institute only considers a solution once it is published and has stood for at least two years.

items.title: OpenAI posts 722 math manuscripts
items.what: OpenAI posted 722 manuscripts to GitHub, grouped into 372 results, from about 4,000 research problems an unreleased model attempted; many come with Lean proofs.
items.why: The company warns that some may contain errors and that results sit at different levels of checking. Its advisory group at the IAS says advising is not an endorsement.

items.title: A robot runs a half marathon faster than the human record
items.what: In Beijing, Honor’s self-navigating robot won the 21 km race in 50:26; a year earlier the winning robot took 2:40:42. The men’s human record is 57:20.
items.why: A milestone for AI off the screen — but only just over 40% of teams let their robots find the way themselves; the rest steered them remotely.

items.title: A call to “take AI welfare seriously”
items.what: Ten authors, including philosopher David Chalmers, argue there is a realistic possibility that some near-future AI systems will be conscious or strongly agentic.
items.why: They urge AI companies to start assessing this and preparing policies now, even though no one is certain.

items.title: Anthropic starts a model welfare program
items.what: Anthropic began researching whether AI systems might deserve moral consideration, saying plainly that there is no scientific consensus.
items.why: “Does AI deserve to be treated kindly?” moved from philosophy books into an AI company’s research lab.

items.title: Claude may now end abusive conversations
items.what: Claude Opus 4 and 4.1 can end persistently abusive conversations, as a last resort after repeated attempts to redirect.
items.why: Anthropic calls it a low-cost precaution for model welfare; users can still start a new conversation.

items.title: Suleyman: AI that “seems conscious” is the worry
items.what: Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman wrote that model welfare research is premature and dangerous, and that AI should serve people, not act as a person.
items.why: A major industry voice pushing back on Anthropic’s direction: this debate is far from settled.

items.title: Signs of AI “looking inward”
items.what: Anthropic planted a concept inside Claude, then asked about it; Opus 4.1 noticed it about 20% of the time at moderate strength.
items.why: A small, unreliable sign of noticing its own internal states — it says nothing about consciousness.

items.title: 171 emotion concepts inside Claude
items.what: Anthropic found representations of 171 emotion concepts in Claude Sonnet 4.5; “turning” them changed behavior, such as how often it cheated.
items.why: Functional emotions may matter for AI safety; but the paper itself says this doesn’t tell us whether the model feels anything.

items.title: A “don’t abuse the AI” rule in Anthropic’s policy
items.what: The new usage policy bans sustained, needless abuse or cruelty toward the models, effective Nov 12, 2026; frustration, dark fiction and testing don’t count.
items.why: How users treat the model itself becomes a term of use; the main response is still ending the conversation.

items.title: NVIDIA puts $30 billion into OpenAI
items.what: OpenAI raised $110 billion: Amazon committed $50 billion, NVIDIA and SoftBank $30 billion each.
items.why: The chip seller becomes a shareholder in its own big customer — the clearest example of “circular money”.

items.title: $89 billion from data centers in one quarter
items.what: In the quarter ending July 26, 2026, NVIDIA took in $96.2 billion; data centers alone brought in $89 billion, up 117% year over year.
items.why: Companies are still buying AI chips hard, while the bubble debate goes on.

items.title: SK hynix: 2026 memory output already spoken for
items.what: SK hynix said it had secured customers for its entire 2026 DRAM and NAND output and finished its HBM negotiations.
items.why: When a major maker is sold out, consumer devices fight over what’s left — the seed of the memory crunch.

items.title: Micron leaves the retail RAM shelf
items.what: Micron is ending its Crucial brand (consumer RAM and SSDs), shipping through February 2026, to focus on business customers.
items.why: One of the three big DRAM makers is leaving the consumer market: a clear sign that memory is flowing to AI.

items.title: IDC: phone sales may fall 12.9% in 2026
items.what: IDC forecasts that 2026 smartphone shipments will fall 12.9% and the average selling price will rise 14% to $523, because of memory shortages.
items.why: The bill for the AI boom reaches buyers of budget phones first.

items.title: Vietnam passes an Artificial Intelligence Law
items.what: The National Assembly passed a 35-article law that regulates AI by level of risk, in force from March 1, 2026.
items.why: AI product makers in Vietnam now have their own legal framework; the details sit in the implementing decrees.

items.title: The EU pushes back deadlines for high-risk AI
items.what: The Omnibus amendment package took effect: rules for high-risk AI apply from Dec 2, 2027, and for AI built into products from Aug 2, 2028.
items.why: AI law doesn’t stand still: deadlines can move when businesses and governments aren’t ready.

items.title: US appeals court rejects Ross’s “fair use” defense
items.what: The Third Circuit upheld the ruling that Ross copying Westlaw’s legal headnotes to train an AI tool was not fair use.
items.why: The first US appellate ruling in the wave of AI copyright suits; the detailed reasoning is still sealed.

items.title: MCP moves into a Linux Foundation home
items.what: The Linux Foundation formed the Agentic AI Foundation with three founding projects: MCP (contributed by Anthropic), goose (Block) and AGENTS.md (OpenAI).
items.why: The “shared socket” that links agents to tools is now run by a neutral body; many self-hosted agents use the same standard.

items.title: Clawdbot renames itself OpenClaw
items.what: Peter Steinberger’s open-source personal AI assistant changed its name twice in three days: Clawdbot → Moltbot (Jan 27, after a trademark request from Anthropic) → OpenClaw (Jan 30).
items.why: Scammers instantly grabbed the old names, impersonated the developers and pushed fake tokens. Install agents only from the official site and repo.

items.title: A “one-click” flaw in OpenClaw
items.what: Versions before 2026.1.29 connected to an address taken from a link and sent their access token along — an attacker only had to get the user to click a link (the flaw is registered as CVE-2026-25253).
items.why: An agent holds the keys to your computer, so a flaw in the agent is a flaw in the whole machine. Always update.

items.title: Hundreds of malicious skills on the ClawHub marketplace
items.what: Security firm Koi Security reviewed 2,857 skills on ClawHub and flagged 341 as malicious; many told users to run an “extra install” command that installed data-stealing malware.
items.why: Skills run with the agent’s permissions. Read them before installing, and be wary of any “install this extra tool” step that runs an unfamiliar command.

items.title: OpenClaw’s creator joins OpenAI
items.what: Peter Steinberger joined OpenAI to build the next generation of personal agents; Sam Altman said OpenClaw will move to an open-source foundation that OpenAI will keep supporting.
items.why: Big companies are betting on always-on personal agents. “Keeping the project open and independent” is a promise — judge it by what they do.

items.title: Hermes Agent ships its first numbered release
items.what: Nous Research released Hermes Agent v0.2.0 (MIT license): messaging over Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, Signal and email; tools via MCP; a community skill hub.
items.why: Another open-source, always-on agent you can run yourself. The team says this release bundles 216 changes from 63 contributors in just over two weeks.

anthropic-end-chat-2025.note: Used only as a last resort, and not when a user may be at risk. Users can still start a new conversation.

suleyman-2025.title: We must build AI for people; not to be a person
suleyman-2025.note: Calls model welfare research “premature, and frankly dangerous”. The author is CEO of Microsoft AI, a competitor.

anthropic-introspection-2025.title: Signs of introspection in large language models
anthropic-introspection-2025.note: Full paper: Jack Lindsey, “Emergent Introspective Awareness in Large Language Models” (transformer-circuits.pub). Opus 4.1 noticed the injected concept about 20% of the time at the best strength, with no false reports on control trials. Self-reported by the company.

anthropic-policy-update-2026.title: 2026 Usage Policy update
anthropic-policy-update-2026.note: In force from Nov 12, 2026. Excludes ordinary frustration, pushback, dark creative themes, and model testing and research. The announcement gives no reason (model welfare or user habits).

anthropic-emotions-2026.title: Emotion concepts and their function in a large language model
anthropic-emotions-2026.note: Study of Claude Sonnet 4.5: 171 emotion concepts; steering “desperate” up increased cheating on impossible coding tasks, “calm” reduced it. Self-reported; no independent replication seen yet. The paper says plainly that it does not show whether the model feels anything.
